reference.source: Cummings Otolaryngology - Head and Neck Surgery
clinicalPearls: The most common congenital midline neck cyst, arising from remnants of the thyroglossal duct along the thyroid's embryological descent
Typically presents as a smooth, painless midline or paramedian swelling near the hyoid bone, often in childhood
Characteristically moves upward with swallowing and with tongue protrusion because of its attachment to the hyoid and tongue base
May present acutely when infected, becoming tender and enlarged, sometimes discharging via a sinus
Ultrasound is used to characterise the cyst and, importantly, to confirm the presence of a normal orthotopic thyroid gland
Rarely the cyst contains the only functioning thyroid tissue, so demonstrating a normal thyroid before surgery is essential
Definitive treatment is excision including the central portion of the hyoid bone and the tract to the foramen caecum (Sistrunk procedure) to minimise recurrence
Papillary thyroid carcinoma can rarely arise within a thyroglossal duct cyst
reference.pathophysiology: During embryogenesis the thyroid gland descends from the foramen caecum at the tongue base to its final pretracheal position, leaving behind the thyroglossal duct, which normally involutes. Persistence of epithelial remnants of this duct allows a cyst to form anywhere along the tract, most often at or just below the hyoid bone in the midline. Because the tract passes intimately through the body of the hyoid, the cyst elevates with swallowing and tongue protrusion. Retained secretions expand the cyst, and communication with the oral cavity predisposes to infection.
additionalDifferentials: Dermoid or epidermoid cyst of the midline neck
Enlarged delphian or submental lymph node
Thyroid nodule or pyramidal lobe lesion
Branchial cleft cyst when more lateral
Plunging ranula or other cystic neck lesion
additionalInvestigations: Neck ultrasound to characterise the cyst and confirm a normal orthotopic thyroid gland
Thyroid function tests where ectopic or absent thyroid is a concern
Cross-sectional imaging (CT or MRI) in atypical or recurrent cases
Fine-needle aspiration cytology if malignancy or an atypical mass is suspected
Radionuclide thyroid scanning when ectopic functioning tissue must be excluded
redFlags: Solid or irregular components, or fixation, suggesting malignancy within the cyst
Acute infection with abscess formation and airway or swallowing compromise
Imaging showing the cyst may contain the only functioning thyroid tissue
reference.prognosis: Excision by the Sistrunk procedure gives a low recurrence rate, whereas simple cystectomy that leaves the tract or hyoid segment recurs more often. Carcinoma within a thyroglossal duct cyst is rare and, when confined, generally has a favourable outlook.
pitfalls: Proceeding to surgery without confirming a normal thyroid gland and inadvertently removing the only functioning thyroid tissue
Performing simple excision rather than removing the central hyoid and tract, leading to recurrence
Repeated incision and drainage of an infected cyst instead of definitive excision once settled
Overlooking malignant transformation in a cyst with solid components
